newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Exiled ex-King hails Romania new leaders.
newsitem.headline: Exiled ex-King hails Romania new leaders.

text.p: Romania's exiled ex-King Michael on Tuesday hailed the election victory of reformers over ex-communists who had blocked his homecoming and pledged to defend his country's interest worldwide.

"You have shown the world and especially our European allies that Romania is a democratic country," Michael told Romanians in a statement issued from his headquarters in Switzerland and sent to local media.
Ex-communist president Ion Iliescu, beaten in Sunday's runoff ballot by reformist Emil Constatinescu, had painted his Christian Democrat rival as a closet monarchist.

"This is not the time for interminable legal or constitutional disputes," the former monarch said, ending months of silence over the accusations which set the tone of the outgoing president's aggressive campaign.

Iliescu and leftwingers from his Party of Social Democracy, also beaten in parliamentary elections, had used the monarchy theme to try to scare voters away from Constantinescu's Democratic Convention bloc.
"A monarch's role is not to interfere in politics," an aide to Michael said by telephone from Versoix, Switzerland, asked to comment on the king's prolonged silence.
Iliescu campaign videos juxtaposed Constantinescu, a bearded academic, with Michael, dethroned and exiled in 1947 by Moscow-backed communists who seized power in Romania.

Small planes dumped leaflets periodically over the capital during the campaign, warning Romanians that Constantinescu would restore the monarchy -- a grave accusation in a country defined as a republic under a post-communist constitution.
Constantinescu, a geology professor with no political career under the Communists, vigorously denied he was a monarchist.
"You surely don't think I'm running in this election in order to relinquish power to somebody else," Constantinescu snapped during one of several televised debates with Iliescu.
The Convention's main components are Constantinescu's Peasant-Christian Democratic Party and liberals. But it also includes small anti-Communist groups, one of them royalist.
The defeated leftist government, voted out seven years after the collapse of communism, had refused to let Michael in since an emotional Orthodox Easter visit in 1992.
That visit drew hundreds of thousands of well-wishers into the streets, prompting the government to insist he could return only as a "commoner".
His last attempt to return home a year ago was thwarted when authorities bundled him back on to a plane at Bucharest airport.
"Romania needs all Romanians, because reconstruction and work for economic development is at its start. I will devote myself to defending our interests in the world," Michael said.
"We are not asking for any favours, but we must find our place within the European Union and NATO, a place which was beyond our reach before your vote."
